blocks.robotComment: Hey, I'm Swipey! 👋 Let's meet a language that gets as close to the machine as it gets. 🤖
blocks.body: C++ (pronounced "C plus plus") is a powerful, general-purpose programming language used to build everything from video games to web browsers to operating systems. It gives you fine-grained control over how a computer uses its memory and processing power — more control than most other popular languages.

code.caption: This is a complete, runnable C++ program. It prints the text "Hello, C++!" to the screen.

blocks.question: What does this program print when it runs?
options: Nothing — it needs more code first
blocks.explanation: std::cout << "Hello, C++!"; sends exactly that text to the screen, so the program prints "Hello, C++!".

blocks.robotComment: No middleman here — your code becomes the program itself. 🏎️
blocks.body: C++ is a "compiled" language: a program called a compiler translates your code directly into machine code — the native instructions a processor understands — which is then packaged into an executable file. Unlike some other languages, C++ does not run inside a virtual machine; once compiled, your program runs straight on the operating system, using the computer's hardware directly.

highlights.text: does not run inside a virtual machine

blocks.robotComment: 🤔 Think about what makes C++ different from languages that use a virtual machine.
blocks.statement: C++ programs run inside a virtual machine, similar to how some other languages work.
blocks.explanation: C++ does not use a virtual machine. It compiles directly to native machine code that runs straight on the operating system.

blocks.robotComment: Objects and raw control, side by side — that combo is very C++. 🧩
blocks.body: C++ supports multiple styles of programming. It can be used in a strictly step-by-step ("procedural") style, but it is best known as an "object-oriented" language — meaning you can build programs out of reusable building blocks called objects, similar to how many modern languages work.

blocks.sentence: A C++ program is translated into machine code by a ___, and does not run inside a virtual machine.
blocks.explanation: A compiler translates C++ source code directly into machine code for the target computer — there is no virtual machine involved.

blocks.robotComment: Every great language starts as somebody's side project — this one's no different. 🛠️
blocks.body: The story of C++ begins in 1979, when a researcher named Bjarne Stroustrup started working at Bell Labs. He loved the C programming language for how fast and close-to-the-hardware it was, but he also missed the organizational tools of another language he had used, called Simula, which introduced the idea of "classes" and objects.

blocks.robotComment: Naming things is hard — even for programming languages. 😄
blocks.body: Stroustrup began adding class-based, object-oriented features on top of C, and originally called his creation "C with Classes". In 1983, the language was renamed "C++" — a playful programmer joke, since "++" is the increment operator in C, meaning "add one". C++ is, quite literally, "one better than C".

blocks.question: What was C++ originally called before it got its current name?
blocks.explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup originally called his language "C with Classes" before it was renamed C++ in 1983.

blocks.sentence: C++ was created by ___ at Bell Labs.
blocks.explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup designed C++, building object-oriented features on top of the C language.

blocks.body: C++ has been continuously standardized since 1998 (a version nicknamed "C++98") by an international committee, so that every compiler maker agrees on the same rules. Major updates followed roughly every few years — C++11 in particular added many modern conveniences, and the committee has kept releasing new versions since, including C++14, C++17, C++20, and C++23.

blocks.robotComment: See if you remember why the name has two plus signs. ➕➕
blocks.statement: The "++" in C++ refers to the increment operator, which means "add one".
blocks.explanation: "++" is C's increment operator. Naming the language "C++" was a joke meaning "one step beyond C".

blocks.robotComment: Nearly 50 years old and still going strong — that's a rare thing in tech. ⏳
blocks.body: Despite being decades old, C++ is still actively maintained and improved today. Because so much critical software was written in it, and because it remains one of the fastest languages available, C++ has never gone out of style — it just keeps evolving.

blocks.robotComment: Picking a first language is a big decision — here's the case for this one. 🎯
blocks.body: C++ has a reputation for being challenging, so why is it still worth learning? The biggest reason: C++ gives you speed and control that few other languages can match. Because it compiles directly to machine code and lets you manage memory yourself, C++ programs can run extremely fast and use resources very efficiently.

blocks.robotComment: Learn to think like the computer, and every other language gets easier. 🧠
blocks.body: C++ also teaches you how computers actually work under the hood — memory, pointers, and performance — in a way that higher-level languages often hide from you. Many programmers say that once you understand C++, picking up other languages feels much easier, because you already understand what is happening beneath the surface.

blocks.question: What is one major reason many programmers learn C++?
options: It gives fine control over performance and memory, and runs extremely fast
It is the only language that can display text on a screen
It automatically writes code for you
It cannot be used to build real applications
blocks.explanation: C++ is prized for its speed, efficiency, and the fine-grained control it gives programmers over memory and hardware.

blocks.sentence: C++ gives programmers unusually fine control over ___ and performance.
blocks.explanation: C++ lets developers manage memory directly, which is a big part of why it can be so fast and efficient.

blocks.robotComment: From mobile games to Mars rovers — the demand is real. 🚀
blocks.body: C++ skills are also in high demand: game studios, financial trading firms, and companies building operating systems or embedded devices (like the software running inside a car or a satellite) all rely heavily on C++. Because so much existing software is already written in it, there is a constant need for people who can read and maintain C++ code.

blocks.statement: C++ is a niche language that almost no companies use anymore.
blocks.explanation: The opposite is true — C++ remains widely used in game development, finance, embedded systems, and many other performance-critical fields.

blocks.robotComment: You're probably using something built with C++ right now. 🌍
blocks.body: C++ quietly powers an enormous amount of the technology you use every day. Here are some of the biggest areas where it shows up.

🎮 Video games: Most major game engines, including Unreal Engine, are written in C++, and countless AAA games are built with it directly. Its speed makes it ideal for rendering graphics and physics in real time.

blocks.question: Why is C++ especially popular for video game development?
options: Its speed and low-level control suit real-time graphics and physics
It is the only language that can draw a triangle on screen
It only runs on gaming consoles
blocks.explanation: C++'s speed and control over hardware resources make it a natural fit for the demanding real-time performance games require.

blocks.robotComment: The software running the internet leans on C++ more than most people realize. 🌐
blocks.body: 🖥️ Web browsers and operating systems: Major parts of browsers like Chrome and Firefox are written in C++, and so are large parts of operating systems like Windows, macOS, and Linux. When software needs to be both fast and reliable at a massive scale, C++ is a common choice.

blocks.sentence: Major parts of web browsers like Chrome and operating systems like Windows are written in ___.
blocks.explanation: C++ is used heavily in the internals of browsers and operating systems, where speed and control matter most.

blocks.body: 💳 Finance and trading systems: High-frequency trading platforms, where decisions must be made in fractions of a millisecond, are frequently built in C++ because of how fast it can execute.

blocks.robotComment: From your car to outer space — C++ gets around. 🛰️
blocks.body: 🔌 Embedded systems: Software running inside cars, medical devices, robots, and even spacecraft is often written in C++, since it can run efficiently on hardware with very limited memory and processing power.

blocks.statement: C++ is only used for small personal hobby projects, never for large, well-known software.
blocks.explanation: C++ is used at a massive scale — in game engines, browsers, operating systems, financial systems, and embedded devices worldwide.

questions.question: How does a C++ program typically run, once it is built?
options: It compiles to machine code and runs directly on the operating system, with no virtual machine
It runs inside a virtual machine, like some other languages
It is interpreted line by line inside a web browser
It only runs inside a spreadsheet application
questions.explanation: C++ compiles directly to native machine code and runs straight on the operating system — there is no virtual machine involved.

questions.explanation: C++ supports multiple styles, including procedural and object-oriented programming.

questions.sentence: C++ was created by ___.
questions.explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup designed C++ at Bell Labs, originally calling it "C with Classes".

questions.question: What was C++ originally called?
questions.explanation: Before being renamed "C++" in 1983, the language was called "C with Classes".

questions.statement: The "++" in C++ is a reference to the increment operator, meaning "add one".
questions.explanation: "++" is C's increment operator — the name is a joke meaning "one step beyond C".

questions.question: Which of these is a major reason people learn C++?
options: It gives fine control over performance and memory
It is the only language capable of printing text
It cannot be used for real, large-scale software
It automatically writes programs for you
questions.explanation: C++ is valued for the speed and low-level control it gives programmers over memory and hardware.

questions.sentence: C++ gives programmers unusually fine control over ___ and performance.
questions.explanation: Manual memory management is a big part of why C++ programs can be so fast and efficient.

questions.statement: Major game engines, such as Unreal Engine, are written in C++.
questions.explanation: C++ is widely used in game development, including major engines like Unreal Engine.

questions.explanation: C++ is used in browsers, operating systems, embedded systems, finance, and many other performance-critical fields.

questions.sentence: High-frequency trading systems often use C++ because it can execute ___.
questions.explanation: C++'s speed makes it well-suited to systems like trading platforms, where decisions must be made in fractions of a millisecond.

blocks.robotComment: Source code is just text you write — several steps turn it into something real. 📝
blocks.body: When you write a C++ program, you type text into a file — for example main.cpp. This human-readable text is called "source code". It follows strict, well-defined rules, but you can still read and understand it as a person.

code.caption: This is C++ source code. You can read and understand it, even if you don't know every detail yet.

blocks.body: A computer processor cannot execute this text directly. A processor only understands "machine code" — raw instructions represented as zeros and ones, specific to its hardware. Source code is an in-between stage: readable by humans, but not yet something the hardware can run.

blocks.robotComment: Think about what a processor actually understands before you answer. 🤔
blocks.statement: A computer processor can run C++ source code directly, without any translation first.
blocks.explanation: A processor only understands machine code. C++ source code must be translated through several steps before it can run.

blocks.body: C++ source code files conventionally use the extension ".cpp" (short for "C plus plus"). Larger programs are often split into multiple .cpp files, plus "header" files (extension ".h" or ".hpp") that share declarations between them.

blocks.sentence: C++ source code files conventionally use the file extension ___.
blocks.explanation: C++ source code is conventionally saved in files ending in ".cpp", such as "main.cpp".

blocks.robotComment: You've got the starting point down — next up, the very first step in turning it into a program. ➡️
blocks.body: In summary: source code is where every C++ program begins. It's the text you write, read, and edit yourself. Turning this text into a running program takes several steps, starting with a tool called the preprocessor, which you'll meet in the next lesson.

blocks.question: What best describes "source code" in C++?
options: The human-readable text you write in a .cpp file
The zeros and ones the processor runs directly
A file that only contains images
A program that installs other programs
blocks.explanation: Source code is the human-written, human-readable text of a program, typically stored in a .cpp file.

blocks.robotComment: Before your code is even compiled, a first pass edits the text itself. ✂️
blocks.body: Before the actual compiler ever looks at your code, C++ runs it through a step called the "preprocessor". The preprocessor scans your source code for special instructions called "directives" — lines that start with a hash symbol "#" — and acts on them before real compilation begins.

The most common directive is "#include", which tells the preprocessor to copy the contents of another file directly into your source code. For example, "#include <iostream>" pulls in the declarations needed to print text to the screen.

code.caption: Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces "#include <iostream>" with the entire contents of that header file.

blocks.question: What does the preprocessor do with a line like "#include <iostream>"?
options: It copies the contents of the iostream header into your source code before compiling
It prints the word "iostream" to the screen when the program runs
It deletes that line permanently from your project
It compiles the file directly into an executable
blocks.explanation: The preprocessor performs text substitution: "#include" is replaced with the full contents of the named file, before the compiler ever runs.

blocks.robotComment: Directives are easy to spot — just look for the # at the start of the line. 🔎
blocks.body: Another common directive is "#define", which can create simple text substitutions of its own, and "#ifdef" / "#endif", which can include or exclude sections of code entirely. All preprocessor directives are handled purely as text — the preprocessor doesn't understand C++ grammar, it just edits the text before the compiler sees it.

blocks.sentence: Preprocessor directives in C++ always begin with the character ___.
blocks.explanation: Every preprocessor directive, such as #include or #define, starts with a hash symbol (#).

blocks.robotComment: Remember: this step happens before the compiler ever gets involved. ⏮️
blocks.statement: The preprocessor runs after the compiler has already translated the code into machine code.
blocks.explanation: It's the other way around: the preprocessor runs first, editing the source text, and only afterward does the compiler translate the result.

blocks.robotComment: Text edited, ready to compile — that's next. ➡️
blocks.body: Once the preprocessor has finished expanding directives like #include, the result is a single, expanded chunk of pure C++ source text — sometimes called a "translation unit" — which is finally ready to be handed to the compiler.

blocks.robotComment: Your expanded source text still needs a translator into real machine instructions. 🔧
blocks.body: Once the preprocessor has finished, the "compiler" takes over. The compiler reads your (now expanded) C++ code and translates it into "object code" — machine instructions specific to your computer's processor. Common C++ compilers include g++ (GCC), clang++, and Microsoft's MSVC.

Unlike some other languages, the C++ compiler translates your code straight toward native machine instructions for your specific processor and operating system — not into some universal, platform-independent middle format. This is one reason C++ programs can run so fast: there is no extra translation step left to do once compiling is done.

code.code: g++ -c main.cpp -o main.o
code.caption: This command tells the g++ compiler to translate main.cpp into an object file called main.o (the "-c" means "compile only, don't link yet").

blocks.sentence: The C++ compiler translates source code into ___ code, made up of native machine instructions.
blocks.explanation: The compiler produces "object code" — machine instructions for a specific processor, saved in an object file.

blocks.robotComment: Not quite a finished program yet — there is one more piece missing. 🧩
blocks.body: The output of the compiler is stored in an "object file" (extension ".o" on Linux/macOS, ".obj" on Windows). Importantly, an object file on its own usually is not yet a runnable program — especially if your code calls functions defined elsewhere, like printing text to the screen, which live in the standard library.

The compiler also checks your code for errors along the way. If you misspell a keyword, forget a semicolon, or use a variable incorrectly, the compiler stops and reports a "compile error" — no object file is produced until the mistake is fixed.

blocks.question: What happens if your C++ source code contains a mistake, like a missing semicolon?
options: The compiler stops with a compile error and produces no object file
The compiler quietly fixes the mistake for you
The mistake is ignored and the program runs anyway
The preprocessor deletes the entire file
blocks.explanation: A mistake in the code causes a compile error. The compiler reports the problem and does not produce a translated object file until it is fixed.

blocks.robotComment: One more link in the chain before you get a program you can actually run. ➡️
blocks.statement: An object file produced by the compiler is always immediately runnable on its own.
blocks.explanation: An object file often isn't runnable by itself yet — pieces from other object files or libraries usually still need to be combined with it. That's the job of the linker, covered next.

blocks.robotComment: One last step stitches everything into a single runnable program. 🧵
blocks.body: After the compiler produces one or more object files, a tool called the "linker" combines them into a single, complete, runnable program called an "executable". The linker's job is to resolve every reference to a function or variable that lives somewhere else, and stitch all the pieces together.

For example, when your code calls a function like the one behind std::cout to print text, that function's actual machine code lives inside the C++ "standard library", not in your own object file. The linker finds that code and links it into your final program, so the reference actually points somewhere real.

code.code:
g++ main.o -o main
// produces the executable: main (or main.exe on Windows)
code.caption: The linker takes the object file main.o, links in the pieces it needs from the standard library, and produces the executable "main".

blocks.question: What is the linker's main job?
options: To combine object files and needed libraries into a single runnable executable
To translate source code into object code for the first time
To fix typos in your source code automatically
To open a web browser and display your program
blocks.explanation: The linker combines one or more object files, along with any library code they depend on, into one finished, runnable executable.

blocks.sentence: The linker combines object files and libraries into a single runnable ___.
blocks.explanation: The end result of linking is an executable file — a complete program ready to run.

blocks.robotComment: Forget a piece and the linker will tell you exactly what is missing. ⚠️
blocks.body: If the linker cannot find the code for something your program refers to — for example, you call a function that was never actually defined anywhere — it reports a "linker error", separate from a compiler error. This can happen even when your code has perfectly valid syntax.

blocks.robotComment: Keep the pipeline order straight in your head: preprocess, compile, then...? 🧠
blocks.statement: Linking happens before compiling in the C++ build process.
blocks.explanation: The order is: preprocess, then compile each file into object code, and only then link the object files together into an executable.

blocks.robotComment: That's the full journey, start to finish. 🏁
blocks.body: In summary, a C++ program goes through four stages before it can run: the preprocessor expands directives, the compiler translates the result into object code, the linker combines object files and libraries into an executable, and finally the operating system runs that executable directly — no virtual machine involved at any point.

questions.question: What is C++ source code?
options: The human-readable text you write in a .cpp file
The zeros and ones the processor runs directly
A file that only contains images
A program that installs other programs
questions.explanation: Source code is the human-written, human-readable text of a program, typically stored in a .cpp file.

questions.sentence: C++ source code files conventionally use the extension ___.
questions.explanation: C++ source code is conventionally saved in files ending in ".cpp".

questions.statement: The preprocessor runs before the compiler translates the code.
questions.explanation: The preprocessor expands directives like #include first; only then does the compiler translate the result.

questions.question: What does the "#include" directive do?
options: It copies the contents of another file into your source code before compiling
It prints text to the screen when the program runs
It permanently deletes a line of code
It compiles a file directly into an executable
questions.explanation: The preprocessor replaces "#include" lines with the full contents of the named file, before compiling begins.

questions.sentence: Preprocessor directives always begin with the character ___.
questions.explanation: Every preprocessor directive, such as #include or #define, starts with a hash symbol (#).

questions.question: What does the C++ compiler produce from your source code?
options: Object code containing native machine instructions
questions.explanation: The compiler translates C++ source code directly into object code — native machine instructions for the target processor.

questions.statement: An object file produced by the compiler is always immediately runnable on its own.
questions.explanation: An object file often still needs to be combined with other object files or libraries by the linker before it can run.

questions.sentence: The ___ combines object files and libraries into a single runnable executable.
questions.explanation: The linker resolves references between object files and libraries and produces the final executable.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the C++ build process?
questions.explanation: The source code is first preprocessed, then compiled into object code, and finally linked into an executable.

questions.statement: C++ programs run inside a virtual machine, similar to some other languages.
questions.explanation: C++ compiles directly to native machine code and runs straight on the operating system, with no virtual machine involved.

blocks.robotComment: Functions are how C++ programs stay organized instead of turning into one giant mess. 🧱
blocks.body: A C++ program is built out of "functions" — named, reusable blocks of code that perform a specific task. Instead of writing the same instructions over and over, you can define a function once and then "call" it wherever you need that task done.

code.caption: A function named "addNumbers" that takes two whole numbers and returns their sum.

blocks.body: Every function has a few key parts: a return type (what kind of value it hands back, such as "int" for a whole number, or "void" for nothing at all), a name, a list of parameters in parentheses (the inputs it accepts), and a body in curly braces { } containing the statements it runs.

blocks.question: What is a function in C++?
options: A named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task
A type of variable that only stores text
A comment that the compiler ignores
A file extension used for C++ programs
blocks.explanation: A function is a reusable, named block of code — you define it once and can call it as many times as needed.

blocks.robotComment: The word 'void' shows up a lot — it just means 'nothing to hand back'. 📭
blocks.body: A function that does not return any value uses the return type "void". For example, a function whose entire job is to print something to the screen usually returns "void", since it doesn't need to hand any value back to whoever called it.

code.caption: This function prints a greeting and returns nothing, so its return type is "void".

blocks.sentence: A function that does not return any value uses the return type ___.
blocks.explanation: "void" is the return type used for a function that hands back no value at all.

blocks.statement: A function can be reused by calling it multiple times, instead of rewriting its code each time.
blocks.explanation: That is the whole point of a function: write the logic once, then reuse it by calling the function wherever needed.

blocks.robotComment: One very special function is coming up next — every C++ program needs it. ➡️
blocks.body: Every C++ program is a collection of one or more functions. But there is exactly one function that every single C++ program must have — the one where the program actually begins running. That function is called main(), and it's the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.robotComment: Every C++ program needs exactly one starting line — this is it. 🚀
blocks.body: Every C++ program needs a starting point — a place where execution begins. That starting point is one very specific function called main(). When your program is launched, the operating system looks for this function and starts running the code inside it.

code.caption: As soon as this program starts, execution begins inside the main() function.

blocks.body: The line "int main()" is called the function's signature. "int" means main() returns a whole number to the operating system when the program finishes — this number is called the "exit status" or "exit code". By convention, "return 0;" means the program finished successfully; any other number typically signals that something went wrong.

blocks.question: What does the operating system look for to start a C++ program?
options: The first line in the source code, whatever it says
The longest function in the entire program
blocks.explanation: Execution of a C++ program always begins inside the function called main() — that is the required entry point.

blocks.robotComment: Zero means "all good" — worth remembering. ✅
blocks.body: You will often see "return 0;" as the very last line inside main(). This sends the number 0 back to the operating system, signaling that the program completed without errors. Some compilers will even assume "return 0;" for you if you leave it out of main() specifically, but it's good practice to write it yourself.

blocks.sentence: Execution of every C++ program begins inside the ___ function.
blocks.explanation: The main() function is the required entry point — every C++ program starts running there.

blocks.statement: A C++ program can have more than one main() function.
blocks.explanation: A C++ program must have exactly one main() function — it is the single, unique starting point.

blocks.robotComment: Next up: what exactly counts as a 'statement' inside a function like main(). ➡️
blocks.body: Inside main(), you write your program's actual instructions — its statements — which run one after another, in order. We'll look closely at what a "statement" is in the next lesson.

blocks.robotComment: A semicolon is C++'s way of saying 'done with this thought.' ✅
blocks.body: A C++ program is made up of many small statements. A statement is a single instruction to the computer — for example "print this text" or "add these two numbers". Every statement ends with a semicolon ";".

code.code: std::cout << "Hello, C++!";
code.caption: This is a single statement. It ends with a semicolon — the character that tells the compiler "this instruction is complete".

blocks.robotComment: Forget this tiny character and the compiler gets confused fast. ⚠️
blocks.body: The semicolon works like a period at the end of a sentence: it tells the compiler "this statement is finished, the next one follows". Leave it out, and the compiler won't know where one statement ends and the next begins — it will report an error.

code.caption: Here are three statements in a row. C++ runs the first one, then the second, then the third — in exactly that order.

blocks.statement: Every statement in C++ must end with a semicolon.
blocks.explanation: A semicolon marks the end of every statement in C++. Without it, the compiler cannot tell where a statement ends.

blocks.robotComment: No shortcuts yet — C++ just runs your code top to bottom. ➡️
blocks.body: At its core, a C++ program is simply a sequence of statements. The processor runs them strictly in order — from top to bottom, one after another. At this stage, there are no "shortcuts" or jumps yet — it's purely step-by-step execution.

blocks.question: Which character marks the end of a statement in C++?
blocks.explanation: A semicolon (;) marks the end of every statement in C++.

blocks.body: Statements don't float around freely — they always sit inside a block enclosed by curly braces { }, such as the body of the main() function. You'll see exactly how these blocks work in the next lesson.

blocks.sentence: C++ executes a program's statements in order, from ___ to bottom.
blocks.explanation: C++ processes statements strictly in the order they appear in the code — from top to bottom.

blocks.robotComment: Curly braces are how C++ knows where a group of code starts and ends. 🧱
blocks.body: Curly braces { } group multiple statements together into a shared "block" in C++. A block marks a clear beginning and end — for example, the body of a function like main().

code.caption: The opening brace right after "int main()" and the closing brace at the end mark the block that is the body of main().

blocks.robotComment: See how one block can live neatly inside another. 📦
blocks.body: Blocks can be nested inside one another, like a box inside another box. For example, the block belonging to an "if" statement can sit entirely inside the block of the function that contains it — it starts later and ends earlier than the surrounding block.

code.caption: Marked with comments: the "if" block sits entirely within the block belonging to main().

blocks.question: What are curly braces { } used for in C++?
options: To group related statements into a block
blocks.explanation: Curly braces { } group statements into a block, such as the body of a function.

blocks.robotComment: Miss a closing brace and the compiler will let you know. ⚠️
blocks.body: Every opening brace { must eventually have a matching closing brace }. If one is missing, the compiler can't tell where a block ends, and it reports an error — even if the rest of the code is otherwise correct.

blocks.statement: Every opening curly brace { needs a matching closing brace }.
blocks.explanation: In C++, braces must always come in matching pairs. If a closing brace is missing, the code won't compile.

blocks.body: As a reminder: main() is itself a block, and the individual statements from the previous lesson sit inside it. As programs grow, you'll see many more blocks nested inside one another — but the core rule never changes: every { needs a matching }.

blocks.sentence: A block that sits entirely within another block is said to be ___ inside it.
blocks.explanation: When one block of curly braces sits completely within another, it is described as "nested" inside it.

blocks.robotComment: Time to pull together everything you have learned about the rules. 📋
blocks.body: You now know about the preprocessor, functions, the main() function, statements, and code blocks. Let's summarize a few basic syntax rules that apply to every C++ program.

code.code:
std::cout << "Hello!"; // correct
Std::Cout << "Hello!"; // Error! C++ is case-sensitive
code.caption: C++ is "case-sensitive" — capitalization matters. "cout" and "Cout" are two completely different names as far as C++ is concerned.

blocks.robotComment: Case matters everywhere in C++ — no exceptions. 🔠
blocks.body: This applies to everything in C++: function names, variable names, keywords like "int" or "return". A single letter with the wrong capitalization leads to a compiler error.

Another fixed rule: every #include directive and every statement plays a specific role, and the pieces must appear in a sensible order — for example, you must #include <iostream> before you can use std::cout, since that's where std::cout is declared.

code.caption: The #include line must come before std::cout is used — the compiler reads your file from top to bottom.

blocks.statement: C++ is case-sensitive (for example, "cout" and "Cout" are different).
blocks.explanation: C++ is case-sensitive: capitalization matters everywhere, including keywords, function names, and variable names.

blocks.body: Indentation — spaces at the start of a line that visually shift nested blocks inward — is not required by the compiler. C++ compiles code without any indentation just fine. Still, you should always indent your code cleanly, because it makes nested blocks far easier for people to read.

code.caption: This code compiles just fine — it's simply much harder to read without indentation than the indented version above.

blocks.question: Which statement about indentation in C++ is correct?
options: It is not required by the compiler, but it makes the code far more readable
The compiler requires exactly four spaces of indentation
Without indentation, the code won't compile
Indentation replaces the semicolon at the end of a statement
blocks.explanation: Indentation only serves human readability. The C++ compiler doesn't require it — semicolons and curly braces are the actual rules that matter to it.

blocks.robotComment: You now have the complete rulebook for any C++ program. 📖
blocks.body: In summary, every C++ program follows these rules: any needed #include directives come first, execution starts in the main() function, every statement ends with a semicolon, related statements sit inside a block of curly braces, and C++ is case-sensitive throughout.

blocks.sentence: To use std::cout for printing text, you must first ___ the iostream header.
blocks.explanation: The line "#include <iostream>" makes the declarations for std::cout available before you use it.

questions.question: What is a function in C++?
options: A named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task
A type of variable that only stores text
A comment that the compiler ignores
A file extension used for C++ programs
questions.explanation: A function is a reusable, named block of code — you define it once and can call it as many times as needed.

questions.sentence: A function that does not return any value uses the return type ___.
questions.explanation: "void" is the return type used for a function that hands back no value at all.

questions.statement: Every C++ program must have exactly one main() function.
questions.explanation: main() is the required, unique entry point of every C++ program.

questions.question: What does "return 0;" at the end of main() typically signal?
options: The compiler found a syntax error
questions.explanation: By convention, returning 0 from main() signals that the program completed without errors.

questions.sentence: Execution of every C++ program begins inside the ___ function.
questions.explanation: main() is the required entry point — every C++ program starts running there.

questions.question: Which character marks the end of a statement in C++?
questions.explanation: A semicolon (;) marks the end of every statement in C++.

questions.statement: C++ executes a program's statements from top to bottom, in order.
questions.explanation: Without jumps or shortcuts, C++ runs statements strictly in the order they appear, from top to bottom.

questions.question: What are curly braces { } used for in C++?
options: To group related statements into a block
questions.explanation: Curly braces { } group statements into a block, such as the body of a function.

questions.sentence: A block that sits entirely within another block is said to be ___ inside it.
questions.explanation: When one block of curly braces sits completely within another, it is described as "nested" inside it.

questions.statement: C++ is case-sensitive, so "cout" and "Cout" are treated as different names.
questions.explanation: C++ is case-sensitive: capitalization matters everywhere, including keywords, function names, and variable names.

blocks.robotComment: Time to make C++ actually say something on screen. 🔊
blocks.body: To display text on the screen (the "console") in C++, you use std::cout together with the << ("insertion") operator. Whatever you put after << gets sent to the console. To use it, your file needs #include <iostream> at the top — that line pulls in the standard input/output library.

code.caption: A complete, runnable C++ program. It prints exactly one line: Hello, C++!

blocks.question: What does this program print when you run it?
options: Nothing — it needs more code first
blocks.explanation: std::cout << sends whatever follows it to the console. Here that is the text "Hello, C++!", so that is exactly what gets printed.

blocks.robotComment: That little std::endl does two jobs at once. 📏
blocks.body: std::endl inserts a newline, just like pressing Enter, so the next output starts on a fresh line below it. It also does something extra: it "flushes" the output buffer, forcing any pending text to actually appear on screen right away. Most of the time you can also use the escape sequence "\n" instead — it inserts the same newline character, but without forcing a flush.

code.caption: Both lines end up on their own row — std::endl and "\n" both start a new line for whatever comes next.

blocks.sentence: The stream manipulator ___ inserts a newline and also forces the output buffer to flush immediately.
blocks.explanation: std::endl inserts a newline just like "\n", but it additionally flushes the stream. Because flushing has a small performance cost, many C++ programmers prefer "\n" when writing lots of output quickly, such as inside a loop.

blocks.robotComment: That std:: prefix is just an address label, nothing scary. 📬
blocks.body: std:: means "this comes from the std namespace" — the part of C++'s standard library where things like cout and endl live. You will sometimes see files that start with using namespace std; so they can write cout instead of std::cout everywhere. This course writes std:: explicitly, since it makes it obvious exactly where each name comes from.

blocks.robotComment: 🤔 Think about what the std:: prefix is actually doing here.
blocks.statement: You must write using namespace std; before you are allowed to use std::cout.
blocks.explanation: std::cout already tells the compiler exactly where to find cout, so using namespace std; is never required — it is only a shortcut some programmers use to avoid typing std:: repeatedly.

blocks.robotComment: Next up: making stubborn characters like quotes and tabs behave. ⌨️
blocks.body: You now know how to print plain text with std::cout. Next, you will learn about escape characters — special codes that let you insert things like line breaks, tabs, and quotation marks directly inside a piece of text.

blocks.robotComment: Some characters need a little help to show up in your text. 🔡
blocks.body: Sometimes you want to output something that cannot simply be typed as-is inside a string — for example a line break in the middle of a sentence, or a quotation mark. For this, C++ has "escape characters": a backslash (\) followed by a letter that has a special meaning.

code.caption: \n produces a line break — right in the middle of a single string.

blocks.sentence: The escape character ___ produces a line break in the middle of a string.
blocks.explanation: \n stands for "newline" and produces a line break, even inside a single string passed to std::cout.

blocks.body: The escape character \t produces a tab — a larger, even amount of spacing. This lets you roughly align text into columns.

code.caption: \t makes sure "Max" and "17" line up roughly underneath each other, even though "Name:" and "Age:" have different lengths.

blocks.question: What is the escape character \t used for?
blocks.explanation: \t inserts a tab, i.e. a larger, even amount of spacing. This helps align text into columns.

blocks.robotComment: This trick lets a quotation mark live peacefully inside a string. 💬
blocks.body: If you want to output a regular quotation mark in the middle of a string, there is a problem: C++ would think the string ends there. The solution is \" — an "escaped" quotation mark that is treated as plain text instead of the end of the string.

code.caption: Without the backslash before the quotation marks, the string would end too early and the code would fail to compile.

blocks.statement: To output a quotation mark inside a string, you write \" instead of just ".
blocks.explanation: Exactly — a plain " would end the string prematurely. With \", the quotation mark is treated as regular text.

blocks.robotComment: Even the backslash needs its own special trick to print itself. ⚙️
blocks.body: And what if you want to output a backslash itself — for example in a file path? Since a single backslash normally starts an escape sequence, you have to double it: \\.

code.caption: Each \\ in the code produces exactly one single backslash in the output.

blocks.robotComment: You've basically got C++'s whole output toolkit now — let's put it all together. 🧰
blocks.body: One of the handiest things about std::cout is that you can chain multiple pieces together in a single statement, one after another, each separated by its own <<. This works for text, numbers, and other values all mixed together — no matter the type, each one just gets sent to the console in order.

code.caption: A single chained statement mixes a string, an int, another string, and a double — all in one line.

blocks.sentence: std::cout lets you combine text and numbers into one line of output by chaining them together with the ___ operator.
blocks.explanation: Each << inserts the next value into the output stream, so you can chain as many as you like in a single statement.

blocks.robotComment: One statement can replace four separate ones. ⚡
blocks.body: You can also combine \n with chaining to print several lines from a single statement, instead of writing a separate std::cout line for each one.

code.caption: A single chained statement with \n produces the exact same output as four separate std::cout statements.

blocks.statement: std::cout << "A\nB"; produces the same output as writing std::cout << "A" << std::endl; followed by std::cout << "B";.
blocks.explanation: \n produces a line break in the middle of the text, so the result looks exactly as if you had used two separate statements.

blocks.body: With \t you can make multiple lines look like a small table by aligning text into columns.

code.caption: Each line begins with a word followed by \t — this makes the prices roughly line up into a column.

blocks.question: Why do you use \t at the same spot in multiple consecutive lines?
options: To align the text into columns, like in a small table
To make the program run faster
To deliberately trigger a compiler error
To delete the text before it
blocks.explanation: \t inserts a tab. When it appears at the same spot in multiple lines, the following words roughly line up into columns.

blocks.robotComment: No + needed here — cout just keeps taking more pieces. 🧩
blocks.body: Notice that, unlike some languages, you did not need any special conversion to print quantity or price alongside plain text — std::cout already knows how to turn an int or a double into readable text. You will meet a different way to join text together, using the + operator on std::string, in an upcoming lesson.

questions.question: Which header must you #include to use std::cout?
questions.explanation: <iostream> brings in the standard input/output stream objects, including std::cout.

questions.statement: The << operator is used to send values to std::cout.
questions.explanation: The insertion operator << sends whatever follows it into the output stream.

questions.sentence: std::endl inserts a newline and also forces the output buffer to ___.
questions.explanation: Unlike "\n", std::endl additionally flushes the output stream immediately.

questions.question: What does this code output?

code.code:
std::cout << "A ";
std::cout << "test" << std::endl;

questions.explanation: Neither statement inserts a newline before the second one runs, so both pieces land on the same line: "A test".

questions.statement: \t produces a tab that helps align text into columns.
questions.explanation: \t inserts a larger, even amount of spacing, useful for lining up columns of text.

questions.sentence: To output a quotation mark directly inside a string, you write ___.
questions.explanation: A plain " would end the string early; \" is treated as a literal quotation-mark character instead.

questions.question: Why do you have to write \\ to output a single backslash?
options: Because a single backslash is interpreted as the start of an escape sequence
Because C++ does not allow backslashes at all
Because a single backslash ends the program
questions.explanation: A lone backslash starts an escape sequence, so you must double it to output one literal backslash character.

questions.statement: std::cout << "A\nB"; produces the same visible output as writing "A" and "B" with a newline between them using two statements.
questions.explanation: \n inserts a line break in the middle of the text, producing the same visible result as two separate lines.

questions.question: What does the << operator let you do that is especially convenient in C++?
options: Chain multiple values of different types into a single output statement
Convert a string into a number
Comment out the rest of the line
questions.explanation: You can chain as many << as you like in one statement, mixing text, numbers, and other values freely.

questions.sentence: Using namespace std; is ___ before you can use std::cout, since the std:: prefix already identifies it.
questions.explanation: std::cout is fully qualified on its own; using namespace std; is only an optional convenience shortcut.

blocks.robotComment: Comments won't run, but they might just save future-you a headache. 📝
blocks.body: A comment is a note in the code that the C++ compiler completely ignores. Comments never change what a program does — they exist purely for humans who read the code: yourself a few weeks from now, or teammates who look at your code later.

code.caption: The compiler skips the line with the comment entirely — it has no effect whatsoever on the program.

blocks.statement: Comments are compiled and executed by the C++ compiler like normal code.
blocks.explanation: Comments are completely ignored by the compiler. They have no effect whatsoever on what the program does.

blocks.robotComment: A comment that just repeats the code isn't pulling its weight. 📝
blocks.body: Code you write today, you often don't read again until weeks or months later — and by then you've forgotten why you wrote certain lines the way you did. A good comment immediately explains what's going on, without you having to think through the entire code again.

code.code:
// TODO: Add an evening greeting later
std::cout << "Good morning!" << std::endl;
code.caption: A TODO comment is a reminder to yourself or your team about what still needs to be done later.

blocks.sentence: A comment that marks an open task for later often begins with the word ___.
blocks.explanation: TODO comments are a widely used convention for marking open tasks directly in the code.

blocks.robotComment: This WHY vs WHAT distinction is the whole secret to good comments. 💡
blocks.body: Comments are especially valuable when they explain WHY something is done in the code — not just WHAT is done. The "what" can often be read directly from the code. The "why", on the other hand, exists only in the mind of the person who wrote it.

code.caption: This comment explains the intent behind the code — information you can't tell from the code alone.

blocks.question: What are comments in C++ mainly intended for?
options: For humans who need to read and understand the code
For the compiler, to avoid errors
To make the compiled program run faster
To store values the program uses
blocks.explanation: Comments are aimed at humans. The compiler ignores them completely — they make the program neither faster nor slower.

blocks.robotComment: Two slashes and you're commenting — C++'s simplest kind of note. ✏️
blocks.body: The simplest way to write a comment in C++ is with two forward slashes: //. Everything on the same line after // is completely ignored by the compiler.

code.caption: The line with // is ignored. The line with std::cout runs completely normally.

blocks.body: A single-line comment doesn't have to sit on its own line. It can also appear directly after code on the same line — this is called an "inline comment".

code.code: std::cout << "Hello!" << std::endl; // prints "Hello!" to the console
code.caption: C++ executes the code before the // and simply ignores the rest of the line after it.

blocks.sentence: A single-line comment in C++ begins with the characters ___.
blocks.explanation: Two forward slashes (//) start a single-line comment in C++.

blocks.robotComment: Turning off code without deleting it is a handy trick. 🔌
blocks.body: With //, you can also temporarily "turn off" an entire line of code without deleting it. This is called "commenting out". The compiler then treats that line as if it weren't there at all.

code.caption: "Line 2" is never printed because the line is commented out. Only "Line 1" and "Line 3" appear.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The middle line is commented out and therefore skipped. Only "A" and "C" are printed.

blocks.robotComment: One small catch about how far a // comment actually reaches. 👀
blocks.body: Important: // only comments out text up to the end of the current line. A line break automatically ends the comment — the next line is read as normal code again.

blocks.statement: A // comment automatically also applies to the next line of code.
blocks.explanation: A // comment automatically ends at the end of the line. The next line is treated as normal code again.

blocks.robotComment: Sometimes one line just is not enough room to explain yourself. 📄
blocks.body: Sometimes a single line isn't enough to explain something. For longer comments, C++ has a second notation: the multi-line comment. It begins with /* and ends with */ — everything in between is ignored, no matter how many lines it spans.

code.caption: Everything between /* and */ is ignored by the compiler — even across multiple lines.

blocks.robotComment: This style is perfect for describing a whole file right at the top. 🗂️
blocks.body: Multi-line comments are especially well-suited for longer explanations — for example, to describe at the beginning of a file what a program actually does.

code.caption: The asterisks (*) at the start of each line are just a visual convention many C++ programmers follow. For the compiler, all that matters is that everything sits between /* and */.

blocks.sentence: A multi-line comment in C++ begins with /* and ends with ___.
blocks.explanation: A multi-line comment is opened with /* and must be closed again with */.

blocks.body: Another practical use: with /* */ you can "turn off" multiple lines of code at once, without having to write // in front of every single line.

code.caption: Both "Middle" lines are completely skipped — only "Start" and "End" are actually printed.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The block between /* and */ is completely ignored. Only "Start" and "End" are actually printed.

blocks.robotComment: Forgetting to close this one causes a very confusing kind of bug. ⚠️
blocks.body: An important difference from //: a multi-line comment always has to be closed with */. If you forget it, the compiler treats all the remaining code up to the next */ it finds as a comment — which can silently swallow real code and lead to very confusing errors.

blocks.statement: A multi-line comment /* ... */ can span multiple lines.
blocks.explanation: That's exactly the advantage of /* */ over //: the comment can span any number of lines until it is closed with */.

blocks.robotComment: You know the syntax — now for writing GOOD comments. ✍️
blocks.body: You now know both types of comments in C++: // and /* */. But just as important as the syntax is knowing when and how to use comments effectively. Here are the most important rules for good comments.

Rule 1: Explain the WHY, not the WHAT. Good code is often already self-explanatory — what it does is visible from the code itself. A comment is usually only helpful when it explains the reason behind a decision.

code.caption: Both comments sit above the same line of code — but only the second one provides information the code alone doesn't show.

blocks.statement: The comment "// prints Hello" above std::cout << "Hello" << std::endl; is an example of a good comment.
blocks.explanation: The comment merely repeats what the code already shows clearly. A good comment would instead explain why this line exists.

blocks.robotComment: A comment that lies is worse than no comment at all. ⚠️
blocks.body: Rule 2: Keep comments up to date. When the code changes but the comment doesn't, you end up with an outdated comment. An outdated comment is often worse than no comment at all — it misleads others (and yourself).

code.code:
// Prints the user's first name
std::cout << "Welcome back!" << std::endl;
code.caption: This comment was probably not updated after the code changed — it no longer describes what the line actually does.

blocks.sentence: A comment that no longer matches the current code is called ___.
blocks.explanation: A comment that no longer matches the changed code is outdated — and can be misleading.

blocks.robotComment: Comment overload can actually make code harder to read. 🌀
blocks.body: Rule 3: Don't over-comment. If every single, obvious line gets its own comment, the code becomes more cluttered instead of clearer. Use comments purposefully: to mark sections or to explain truly tricky parts.

code.caption: Comments should appear where they truly provide guidance — not on every simple line.

blocks.question: When is a comment most useful?
options: When it explains why something is done, or usefully marks a section
When it appears before every single line of code
When it simply repeats what the code already shows
When it is as long as possible
blocks.explanation: Comments are most valuable when they provide context or reasons that aren't obvious from the code itself — not when they merely repeat the code.

questions.question: What are comments in C++ mainly intended for?
options: For humans who need to read and understand the code
For the compiler, so it can avoid errors
To make the compiled program run faster
To store values the program uses while it runs
questions.explanation: Comments exist purely for people reading the code. The compiler ignores them completely.

questions.statement: Comments are compiled and executed by the C++ compiler just like normal code.
questions.explanation: The compiler skips comments entirely — they have no effect whatsoever on what the program does.

questions.sentence: A single-line comment in C++ begins with the characters ___.
questions.explanation: Two forward slashes start a single-line comment. Everything after them, up to the end of that line, is ignored.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The middle line is commented out, so it never runs. Only "A" and "C" are printed.

questions.statement: A // comment automatically continues onto the next line of code as well.
questions.explanation: A // comment always ends at the end of its own line. The next line is read as normal code again.

questions.sentence: A multi-line comment in C++ begins with /* and ends with ___.
questions.explanation: A multi-line comment is opened with /* and must always be closed again with */.

questions.question: What happens if you open a /* comment but forget to close it with */?
options: The compiler treats all the following code as comment until it finds the next */
The comment automatically ends at the end of the line
The program runs normally and the comment is ignored
C++ inserts the missing */ for you automatically
questions.explanation: An unclosed /* silently swallows every line after it until a */ turns up, which can hide real code and produce very confusing errors.

questions.statement: The comment "// prints Hello" written above std::cout << "Hello" << std::endl; is an example of a good comment.
questions.explanation: It just repeats what the code already shows. A good comment explains WHY the line is there, not WHAT it plainly does.

questions.sentence: A comment that no longer matches the code it describes is called ___.
questions.explanation: An outdated comment is often worse than no comment at all, because it actively misleads whoever reads it next.

questions.question: When is a comment most useful?
options: When it explains why something is done, or usefully marks a section
When it appears above every single line of code
When it simply restates what the code already shows
When it is as long as possible
questions.explanation: Comments earn their place when they add context the code can't show on its own — not when they repeat it or clutter every line.

blocks.robotComment: Variables are how your program remembers things — let's give data a name. 📦
blocks.body: A variable is a named container that stores a piece of data your program can work with and change while it runs. In C++, every variable must have an explicit type, so the compiler always knows exactly what kind of data it is allowed to hold and how much memory to set aside for it.

code.code:
int age = 25;
std::cout << age << std::endl;
code.caption: Declaring an int variable named age, giving it the value 25, and then printing it.

blocks.robotComment: Notice how this pattern reads almost like a sentence: type, name, value. 🔤
blocks.body: The general pattern for declaring and initializing a variable is: type name = value;. Here, int is the type, age is the name, and 25 is the value assigned with the = operator. You don't have to assign a value right away — you can declare a variable first and assign it later.

blocks.robotComment: This is a real gotcha for people coming from other languages. ⚠️
blocks.body: Here is something to watch out for: unlike some other languages, C++ does NOT automatically give a local variable a safe default value. If you declare a variable without initializing it and then use it, it contains whatever leftover, unpredictable data already happened to be sitting in that spot in memory. This is called undefined behavior, and it compiles just fine — the bug only shows up when the program runs. Always initialize your variables.

code.code:
int score; // dangerous: not initialized
std::cout << score << std::endl; // could print anything

int safeScore = 0; // always initialize instead
std::cout << safeScore << std::endl; // reliably prints 0
code.caption: The first block compiles without error, but score holds a garbage value. The second block is the safe habit to build.

blocks.robotComment: 🤔 This is exactly the trap the last lesson warned you about.
blocks.statement: If you declare a variable in C++ without giving it a value, C++ automatically sets it to a safe default like 0.
blocks.explanation: C++ does not automatically initialize local variables. An uninitialized variable holds unpredictable leftover data — always assign a starting value yourself.

blocks.robotComment: Naming rules feel picky at first, but they make code predictable. 📛
blocks.body: Variable names in C++ must start with a letter or an underscore (_) — never a digit — and cannot be one of C++'s reserved keywords (like int or class). Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables. By convention, this course writes variable names in camelCase: the first word lowercase, and each following word starting with a capital letter, e.g. totalScore or firstName.

blocks.sentence: By convention, variable names in this course use ___, where the first word is lowercase and every following word starts with a capital letter, such as totalScore.
blocks.explanation: camelCase — lowercase first word, capitalized following words, no underscores — is a widely used naming convention for variables in C++.

blocks.body: A variable can also be reassigned: given a new value after it was already initialized. The new value simply replaces the old one — the old value is gone. You never repeat the type when reassigning, only when first declaring the variable.

code.caption: Reassigning a variable using its own current value is a very common pattern, for example when tracking a countdown.

blocks.robotComment: A handful of built-in types carry almost all the data in C++. 🧮
blocks.body: Every variable in C++ needs a type, and the primitive (or "fundamental") types are the most basic kinds of data a variable can hold. They store a simple value directly in memory, which makes them fast and memory-efficient.

code.caption: Four commonly used primitive types: a whole number, a decimal number, a true/false value, and a single character.

blocks.robotComment: Four everyday types, four different jobs. 🔡
blocks.body: int stores whole numbers (no decimal point) and is the default choice for counting things. double stores decimal numbers and is the default choice for anything with a fractional part, like prices or measurements. bool can only ever be true or false, which makes it perfect for yes/no conditions. char stores exactly one character, written in single quotes like 'A' — never double quotes, which are reserved for std::string.

blocks.sentence: To store a single character like 'A', you use the ___ type, written with single quotes.
blocks.explanation: char stores exactly one character and uses single quotes, unlike std::string which uses double quotes and can hold many characters.

blocks.body: C++ also has smaller and larger whole-number types for when int isn't the right fit: short saves memory for small numbers, while long and long long are used for whole numbers bigger than int can reliably hold. float is a smaller, less precise alternative to double, using less memory but storing fewer accurate decimal digits.

code.caption: long long comfortably holds numbers far bigger than int can; float literals are marked with an f suffix.

blocks.robotComment: The exact size can even depend on your computer's compiler. 💻
blocks.body: One quirk of C++: the exact size (in bytes) of a type like int or long is not fixed by the language the same way it is in some other languages — it can vary slightly between compilers and platforms, though int is virtually always at least 4 bytes on modern systems. If you ever need to be certain, the sizeof operator tells you the exact size in bytes on your current setup.

code.code: std::cout << sizeof(int) << std::endl; // commonly prints 4
code.caption: sizeof(int) reports how many bytes an int occupies in memory on this system.

blocks.statement: In C++, a local variable's exact byte size for a type like int is guaranteed to be identical on every computer and compiler in existence.
blocks.explanation: C++ only guarantees a minimum size for most primitive types — the exact size can vary by platform and compiler, even though int is almost always at least 4 bytes today.

blocks.question: Which primitive type would you use to store whether a light switch is on or off?
blocks.explanation: bool is designed exactly for two-state, true/false values like on/off.

questions.question: What is a variable in C++?
options: A named container that stores a piece of data the program can use and change
A note in the code that the compiler ignores
A file that holds the compiled program
A keyword that ends a statement
questions.explanation: A variable is a named container for data. In C++ it always has an explicit type, so the compiler knows exactly what it may hold.

questions.sentence: The general pattern for declaring and initializing a variable in C++ is ___.
questions.explanation: The type comes first, then the name, then an optional starting value assigned with =, for example int age = 25;.

questions.statement: If you declare a local variable in C++ without giving it a value, C++ automatically sets it to a safe default like 0.
questions.explanation: C++ does not initialize local variables for you. An uninitialized variable holds unpredictable leftover data — reading it is undefined behavior.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a valid C++ variable name?
questions.explanation: A variable name must start with a letter or an underscore — never a digit — so 2ndPlayer is rejected by the compiler.

questions.sentence: By convention, this course writes variable names in ___, such as totalScore.
questions.explanation: camelCase starts the first word lowercase and capitalizes each following word, with no underscores.

questions.question: Which primitive type would you use to store whether a light switch is on or off?
questions.explanation: bool holds exactly one of two values, true or false — a perfect fit for an on/off state.

questions.sentence: To store a single character like 'A', you use the ___ type, written with single quotes.
questions.explanation: char stores exactly one character in single quotes. Double quotes are reserved for text, which is std::string's job.

questions.statement: double is the default choice when you need to store a number with a fractional part, such as a price.
questions.explanation: double stores decimal numbers and is preferred over float for everyday use because it keeps more accurate digits.

questions.question: Which type would you reach for to store a whole number far larger than an int can reliably hold?
questions.explanation: long long is the larger whole-number type, while short is the smaller one used to save memory.

questions.statement: In C++, a type like int is guaranteed to occupy exactly the same number of bytes on every computer and compiler.
questions.explanation: C++ only guarantees minimum sizes — the exact byte size can vary by platform and compiler. The sizeof operator reports the real size on your system.

blocks.robotComment: Text needs its own type — here's C++'s answer. 🧵
blocks.body: std::string is the type C++ uses for text made of more than one character. Unlike the primitives you just learned, std::string is not a primitive type — it comes from the standard library, so you need #include <string> at the top of your file to use it.

code.caption: The + operator concatenates (joins) strings together. It works between two std::string values, or between a std::string and plain quoted text.

blocks.robotComment: These come up constantly once you start working with real text. 🔧
blocks.body: std::string comes with many useful member functions. .length() (or its twin, .size()) returns how many characters are in the string. You can also grab a single character by its position — counting from 0 — using square brackets.

code.caption: .length() and square-bracket indexing are some of the most frequently used std::string operations.

blocks.sentence: To find out how many characters are in a std::string called word, you write ___.
blocks.explanation: .length() is called on the string itself with parentheses, and returns the number of characters it contains.

blocks.robotComment: Here's a genuine difference from some other languages. 🔓
blocks.body: Unlike text types in some other languages, std::string is mutable: you can change individual characters after the string is created, using square brackets on the left side of an assignment. You can also compare two strings directly with == — it compares their actual text content, not where they live in memory.

code.caption: Changing word[0] mutates the string in place, and == compares the two strings' text content directly.

blocks.statement: You can compare the text content of two std::string values directly with the == operator.
blocks.explanation: std::string overloads == to compare characters, so a == b is true whenever both strings contain exactly the same text.

blocks.question: What does word[0] = 'B'; do if word currently holds "Cat"?
options: It changes word to "Bat", replacing the first character
It causes a compiler error, since strings cannot change
It adds "B" to the end, making "CatB"
It has no effect at all
blocks.explanation: std::string is mutable, so assigning to word[0] replaces just that character in place, turning "Cat" into "Bat".

blocks.robotComment: Small distinction, but worth remembering. 📌
blocks.body: One last thing to keep straight: a std::string is written with double quotes ("Ada"), while a single char is written with single quotes ('A'). Mixing them up is a very common early mistake — the compiler will complain if you try to put more than one character between single quotes.

questions.question: Which header must you #include before using std::string?
questions.explanation: std::string comes from the standard library, so <string> has to be included before you can use it.

questions.statement: std::string is one of C++'s primitive types, just like int and bool.
questions.explanation: std::string is not primitive — it is a type provided by the standard library, which is why it needs its own #include.

questions.sentence: To find out how many characters a std::string called word contains, you write ___.
questions.explanation: .length() (or its twin .size()) is called on the string itself and returns its number of characters.

questions.question: std::string word = "Code"; What does word[0] give you?
questions.explanation: Square-bracket indexing counts from 0, so word[0] is the very first character: C.

questions.statement: std::string is mutable — you can change an individual character after the string was created.
questions.explanation: Unlike text types in some other languages, assigning to word[0] changes that character in place.

questions.sentence: The ___ operator joins (concatenates) two std::string values into one.
questions.explanation: + concatenates strings, either between two std::string values or between a std::string and plain quoted text.

questions.question: std::string word = "Cat"; word[0] = 'B'; What does word hold afterward?
questions.explanation: Assigning to word[0] replaces just the first character, turning "Cat" into "Bat".

questions.statement: Two separate std::string variables holding identical text compare equal with ==.
questions.explanation: std::string overloads == to compare the actual text content, not where the strings live in memory.

questions.question: What is the difference between "A" and 'A' in C++?
options: "A" is text (std::string), while 'A' is a single char
"A" is a char, while 'A' is text
Single quotes are not valid C++ at all
questions.explanation: Double quotes mark text, single quotes mark exactly one character — mixing them up is a very common early mistake.

questions.sentence: A single char is written with ___ quotes, while a std::string is written with double quotes.
questions.explanation: 'A' is a char; "A" is text. The compiler complains if you put more than one character between single quotes.

blocks.robotComment: Some values should just never change — const makes that a promise. 🔒
blocks.body: Sometimes a value should never change once it's set — think of the number of days in a week, or the maximum number of players allowed in a game. C++ lets you mark a variable as a constant using the const keyword, which tells the compiler this variable's value must never change after it is initialized.

code.code:
const double PI = 3.14159;
std::cout << PI << std::endl;
code.caption: Declaring a constant with const — PI can be read, but never reassigned.

blocks.robotComment: ALL_CAPS names make constants impossible to miss in your code. 🔠
blocks.body: By convention, constant names are often written in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: every letter capitalized, with underscores separating words, such as MAX_PLAYERS or DAYS_IN_WEEK. This makes constants instantly recognizable, setting them apart at a glance from regular camelCase variables.

code.code:
const int MAX_PLAYERS = 4;
std::cout << MAX_PLAYERS << std::endl;
code.caption: MAX_PLAYERS follows the UPPER_SNAKE_CASE convention for constants.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly the kind of bug a good constant name prevents. 🎯
blocks.body: If you try to reassign a const variable after it has been initialized, the code will not compile — the compiler catches the mistake before the program ever runs. This is exactly why constants are so useful: they replace unexplained 'magic numbers' scattered through your code with a single, clearly named, protected value. If that value ever needs to change, you update it in exactly one place.

code.code:
const int MAX_LIVES = 3;
MAX_LIVES = 5; // Compile error: assignment of read-only variable
code.caption: The compiler stops you from ever changing a const variable's value after it is set.

blocks.sentence: The ___ keyword tells C++ that a variable's value can never be changed after it is initialized.
blocks.explanation: const marks a variable as a constant — any attempt to reassign it causes a compile error.

blocks.question: What happens if you try to reassign a variable declared with const?
options: Nothing — const has no real effect
blocks.explanation: Reassigning a const variable is a compile-time error in C++.

blocks.statement: A const variable must be given its value at the moment it is declared, since it can never be assigned afterward.
blocks.explanation: Since a const variable can never be reassigned, it must already be initialized with a value at the point it is declared.

blocks.robotComment: Converting between types isn't always free — some directions are riskier. 🔄
blocks.body: Type casting means converting a value from one type to another. C++ has two kinds: implicit casting, which happens automatically when no data is likely to be lost, and explicit casting, which you write yourself because it risks losing information.

code.caption: This implicit conversion happens automatically because every int value fits perfectly inside a double.

blocks.robotComment: static_cast is C++'s way of making you own the risk. ✍️
blocks.body: Going the other way — from a larger or more precise type to a smaller one, like double to int — risks losing information, so it is good practice to make the conversion explicit using static_cast<targetType>(value). This tells anyone reading the code exactly what conversion is intended.

code.caption: Casting a double to int truncates (cuts off) the decimal part — it does not round.

blocks.robotComment: You may also see this shorter style in older code. 👀
blocks.body: You might also come across an older, C-style cast that looks like (int) price instead of static_cast<int>(price). Both work, but static_cast is the modern, recommended style in C++: it stands out clearly in the code and the compiler can check it more strictly, catching more mistakes at compile time.

code.caption: Both lines produce 9, but static_cast is the style this course recommends going forward.

blocks.sentence: The modern, recommended way to explicitly convert a double to an int in C++ is ___.
blocks.explanation: static_cast<targetType>(value) is the modern C++ syntax for an explicit cast, preferred over the older C-style (int) value.

blocks.robotComment: Overflow bugs are sneaky — the number doesn't error, it just lies. 🐛
blocks.body: Precision loss isn't limited to decimals: casting a whole-number type into a smaller one can also lose data if the value doesn't fit. When that happens, the number can "wrap around" into a completely unexpected — even negative — result, which is a common source of subtle bugs.

code.caption: Casting a value too large to fit into int causes it to overflow instead of simply being cut down.

blocks.question: What does static_cast<int>(9.99) produce?
blocks.explanation: Casting a double to int simply cuts off the decimal part rather than rounding.

blocks.statement: Converting an int to a double happens implicitly in C++, without needing static_cast.
blocks.explanation: Widening an int to a double never loses data, so C++ performs it automatically without requiring an explicit cast.
